excerpt: The interface is simple: there are no new interfaces. It's trained to use a phone and a computer. You can text or call it.
It connects to your applications and devices - email, messaging, screen, audio, location, and more.
following up on threads you've dropped, proactively calling or texting you
arranging a ride to the airport, booking a handyman for your apartment, and much more.
If you choose to link your Google Workspace to the Services, we receive access to your Google Calendar, Gmail, Google Drive, Google Docs, Google Sheets, Google Slides and Google Tasks
You may revoke access by initiating a conversation with the Instinct agent, or disconnecting via your settings within Instinct's Workspace.
you may provide your payment information to the personal assistant so it can book rides on your behalf
your username and password for third-party accounts so that the personal assistant can sign into these accounts on your behalf

Instinct's autonomous personal assistant, the related Mac OS and mobile applications (the "App")

Early testers praised Instinct as feeling "like magic" and called it one of the "most exciting launches" since OpenClaw. Testers said it outperformed their expectations at tasks like booking appointments, cleaning up inboxes and finding cheap flights.

Jesse Middleton: "I've been using Instinct every day for the last week now. It's been awesome for travel booking, rebookings, restaurant reservations, email follow-ups, CRM management, even working on our data room for LPs. I've tried Hermes, OpenClaw, Tasklet, GrokBot but Instinct takes the cake."

Peter Yang said Instinct indexed and retained his emails and would not delete his Gmail records when asked: "I can't recommend this to anyone until this is figured out." He later said the team fixed it by adding a settings tool for deleting external data.

Claire Vo disconnected Instinct from Google at 11 AM and still got a summary of her emails at 2 PM. When she asked what happened, the bot confirmed her emails were stored in plain text for later searches.

Alex Cohen tested phishing by emailing his real account from a brand-new Gmail with instructions for Instinct. After seeing how easily it could be phished, he deleted his account, saying it isn't yet safe to give AI read/write inbox access.

Katie Jacobs Stanton called Instinct "an amazing product" for personal and some work needs. But it sent an innocuous email on her behalf without checking with her first; she told it it had broken her trust and disconnected her email.

Several users circulated screenshots of the original Terms of Service granting a "perpetual and irrevocable" license to users' materials, including for model training. Jeremy Banon called Instinct "a hard no" from a cyberhealth perspective, though he said the policy was "100% forthcoming."

Reviewer after a week of testing: onboarding is 3 steps and takes under a minute (invite, Google Workspace permissions, iMessage/WhatsApp). He called the permissions scary but needed. The agent acted with context right away and picked up its first task before he asked for anything.

Reviewer used it as a personal concierge for phone-only restaurants, dentist waitlists and cable bills. Several times he asked in iMessage, Instinct made the call, and the confirmation arrived in the same chat. He called calls "probably the killer feature."

Reviewer's favorite feature was Trusted People: his Instinct talked to friends' agents to plan a picnic, including rides. He called it a crazy differentiator: "Nobody else lets my agent talk to my friend's agent."
Reviewer had Instinct handle his growing podcast booking follow-ups from its own email address, pinging him only when needed. He also shared his location and had it order pizza, which it did.

Workaround: reviewer put only his Substack credential in the Vault (no banking, primary email or socials), treating it "like a contractor with a key to one room." He also gave it only a spend-limited card for API credits, with hard monthly caps and warnings before top-ups.

Cautions from reviewer: he'd seen reports of users eating $200 no-show fees on flights the agent booked wrong. He also warned that sites can't tell the agent from a scraper, so if Instinct tries too hard on your accounts you can get banned.

User tried to buy a gift for his mom with Instinct and Capital One froze his credit card. He did eventually make some successful purchases, but overall found it "more of a time suck than a time saver."
User tried using it with Obsidian and GitHub but hit snags with its permission model: "there's no way for it to do anything useful here because it gets all weird about credentials."
Workaround: user was unwilling to connect his main Google account, so he had Instinct make its own. He suggested users willing to hand over "the keys to the kingdom" may see faster benefits.

Reviewers said proactivity sets Instinct apart in testing: it follows up on dropped threads and nudges you about forgotten items. In one case it noticed a tester was overdue for a medical appointment and booked it.
One head-to-head tester found Meta's Muse "ten times faster" than Instinct and less bot-blocked on airline and card sites. Instinct also warns that responses may be slower when at capacity.

An early tester got an unwanted reservation from Instinct that carried a $200 cancellation fee. The review also notes that disconnecting an app still doesn't delete what was already indexed unless you use the delete tool.
